sentence: People with asthma may notice chest tightness, wheeze or breathlessness during the pollen season.
NHS sources describe wheeze, shortness of breath or worsening asthma as needing prompt medical attention.
Hay fever is an allergic reaction to pollen from plants.
The reaction usually happens when pollen touches the mouth, nose, eyes or throat.
MedlinePlus, a United States source, names pollen from trees, grasses and ragweed.
Allergy UK describes hay fever as driven by tree, grass and weed pollen.
Tree pollen is usually released first, from late March to mid-May, followed by grass and then weed pollen.
Weed pollen runs longer, with peak levels often in July and August.
Some people react to one type of pollen and then feel better, while others are affected by several.
Some people are allergic to both tree and grass pollen and have symptoms for most of the spring and summer.
Warm, calm, sunny weather raises pollen counts, while cold or cloudy spells reduce them.
Rain clears pollen from the air, so counts tend to fall on wet days.
MedlinePlus says diagnosis usually starts with a physical examination and a history of symptoms.
Skin or blood tests are sometimes added, including blood tests that measure allergy-related substances.

sentence: The NHS says there is no cure for hay fever, but symptoms can be eased.
Pharmacists can recommend antihistamine tablets, drops or nasal sprays, and steroid nasal sprays.
One local NHS page says non-drowsy antihistamines such as cetirizine, loratadine and fexofenadine are the usual first choice.
Older antihistamines such as chlorphenamine are more likely to cause sleepiness.
Steroid nasal sprays can take a few days to work and may be combined with an antihistamine at first.
MedlinePlus describes nasal corticosteroid sprays as the most effective of the main options.
Eye drops containing sodium cromoglicate need regular use to be effective.
Local NHS guidance says GPs generally no longer prescribe oral antihistamines, steroid nasal sprays or these eye drops for hay fever.
They are therefore usually bought from a pharmacy, and local rules vary.
note: Local NHS pages; the summary stressed that rules vary by area
